code.title: ROW_NUMBER vs RANK vs DENSE_RANK and the Nth highest salary
code.python:
import sqlite3

db = sqlite3.connect(":memory:")
db.execute("CREATE TABLE emp(name TEXT, salary INT)")
db.executemany("INSERT INTO emp VALUES (?,?)",
               [("Ann", 300), ("Bob", 200), ("Cy", 200), ("Di", 100)])

# Window functions number rows in salary order; ties show the difference
rows = db.execute("""
  SELECT name, salary,
         ROW_NUMBER() OVER (ORDER BY salary DESC, name) AS rn,
         RANK()       OVER (ORDER BY salary DESC) AS rk,
         DENSE_RANK() OVER (ORDER BY salary DESC) AS dr
  FROM emp ORDER BY rn""").fetchall()
print("name salary row_number rank dense_rank")
for r in rows:
    print(*r)

# Nth highest DISTINCT salary = DENSE_RANK = N.
# The outer SELECT gives NULL (not zero rows) when N is too large.
for n in (2, 9):
    q = """SELECT (SELECT DISTINCT salary FROM
                (SELECT salary, DENSE_RANK() OVER (ORDER BY salary DESC) d FROM emp)
              WHERE d = ?)"""
    print("N =", n, "->", db.execute(q, (n,)).fetchone()[0])

followUps:
Yes: count how many distinct salaries are higher than each row's salary. A row is the Nth highest when exactly N-1 distinct salaries are above it.

SELECT DISTINCT e.salary FROM emp e
WHERE (SELECT COUNT(DISTINCT salary) FROM emp
       WHERE salary > e.salary) = N - 1;

With salaries 300, 200, 200, 100 and N = 2, only 200 has one higher distinct value. Cost is O(n²) as a correlated subquery. The simpler form is ORDER BY salary DESC LIMIT 1 OFFSET N-1 on a DISTINCT subquery, O(n log n).

NULLs are not real salaries, so remove them before ranking or they can be returned as the "highest". Where NULL sorts depends on the database: PostgreSQL and Oracle put it first in a DESC sort, SQLite and MySQL treat it as smallest.

Add WHERE salary IS NOT NULL. Example: 300, NULL, 200 with N = 2 should return 200; in PostgreSQL without the filter the NULL takes rank 1 and the answer would be 300. Comparisons like salary > x are never true for NULL, so the count-based method skips NULLs automatically.

code.title: Top 3 per department with a deterministic tie-breaker
code.python:
import sqlite3

db = sqlite3.connect(":memory:")
db.execute("CREATE TABLE emp(id INT, dept TEXT, salary INT)")
db.executemany("INSERT INTO emp VALUES (?,?,?)", [
    (1, "eng", 90), (2, "eng", 80), (3, "eng", 80), (4, "eng", 70),
    (5, "ops", 60), (6, "ops", 50)])
print("input:", db.execute("SELECT * FROM emp").fetchall())

# ROW_NUMBER with id as tie-breaker gives exactly 3 rows per group
q1 = """
WITH r AS (
  SELECT id, dept, salary,
         ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY dept ORDER BY salary DESC, id) AS rnk
  FROM emp)
SELECT dept, id, salary FROM r WHERE rnk <= 3 ORDER BY dept, rnk"""
print("ROW_NUMBER top 3:", db.execute(q1).fetchall())

# RANK keeps ties (80 and 80 both rank 2, 70 ranks 4, so it is dropped)
q2 = q1.replace("ROW_NUMBER()", "RANK()")
print("RANK top 3:      ", db.execute(q2).fetchall())

followUps:
QUALIFY is a clause that filters on window function results directly, so you do not need a wrapping CTE. It runs after window functions, the way HAVING runs after GROUP BY.

SELECT dept, name, salary FROM emp
QUALIFY ROW_NUMBER() OVER (
  PARTITION BY dept ORDER BY salary DESC) <= 3;

It exists in Snowflake, BigQuery, Teradata and DuckDB, but not in SQL Server, PostgreSQL, MySQL or SQLite, where you use the CTE plus WHERE rnk <= 3 form. The result and cost are the same.

SQLite lets you select a bare column next to MAX() and returns that column from the row holding the max. With ties for the max it returns one of the tied rows, and which one is not guaranteed.

Example: rows (a, 80) and (b, 80) in one dept, SELECT name, MAX(salary) gives either a or b with 80. The rule works only with a single MIN or MAX, not other aggregates. For a deterministic answer use ROW_NUMBER with ORDER BY salary DESC, id.

code.title: Gaps and islands: value minus ROW_NUMBER is constant in a run
code.python:
import sqlite3

db = sqlite3.connect(":memory:")
db.execute("CREATE TABLE t(id INT)")
ids = [1, 2, 3, 7, 8, 10, 11, 12]
db.executemany("INSERT INTO t VALUES (?)", [(i,) for i in ids])
print("ids:", ids)

# Technique A: id - row_number is the same for every row of one island
islands = db.execute("""
  WITH k AS (SELECT id, id - ROW_NUMBER() OVER (ORDER BY id) AS grp FROM t)
  SELECT MIN(id), MAX(id), COUNT(*) FROM k GROUP BY grp ORDER BY 1""").fetchall()
print("islands (start, end, size):", islands)

# Gaps: look at the next id with LEAD; a jump above 1 is a gap
gaps = db.execute("""
  SELECT id + 1, nxt - 1 FROM
    (SELECT id, LEAD(id) OVER (ORDER BY id) AS nxt FROM t)
  WHERE nxt - id > 1""").fetchall()
print("gaps (first missing, last missing):", gaps)
# Cost: one sort, O(n log n) time, O(n) space

followUps:
Duplicates break technique A, because two rows with the same value get different row numbers, so value minus row number drifts and one island splits. Example: ids 1, 2, 2, 3 get row numbers 1, 2, 3, 4 and differences 0, 0, -1, -1, so two islands instead of one.

Fix it by taking DISTINCT values first, or use DENSE_RANK instead of ROW_NUMBER: ids 1, 2, 2, 3 get 1, 2, 2, 3 and the difference stays 0. If duplicates should count toward the island size, COUNT(*) after grouping.

Sort intervals by start, keep a running maximum of all previous ends, and start a new group whenever the next start is greater than that running end. This is technique B.

flag = CASE WHEN start > MAX(end) OVER (ORDER BY start
   ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND 1 PRECEDING)
   THEN 1 ELSE 0 END
grp = SUM(flag) OVER (ORDER BY start)

Example: [1,5], [3,8], [10,12] get groups 1, 1, 2 (the first row has a NULL max, treat it as a new group), so the merged intervals are [1,8] and [10,12]. Use the running MAX, not just the previous end, since one long interval can cover several later ones. Cost O(n log n).

code.title: Users with 3 or more consecutive login days and the longest streak
code.python:
import sqlite3

db = sqlite3.connect(":memory:")
db.execute("CREATE TABLE logins(user_id INT, day TEXT)")
data = [(1, "2024-01-01"), (1, "2024-01-02"), (1, "2024-01-02"), (1, "2024-01-03"),
        (1, "2024-01-05"), (2, "2024-01-10"), (2, "2024-01-12"), (2, "2024-01-13")]
db.executemany("INSERT INTO logins VALUES (?,?)", data)
print("logins:", data)

# DISTINCT first (duplicate logins), then day - row_number = streak key
streaks = db.execute("""
  WITH d AS (SELECT DISTINCT user_id u, day FROM logins),
  k AS (SELECT u, day,
        date(day, '-' || ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY u ORDER BY day) || ' days') AS g
        FROM d)
  SELECT u, MIN(day), MAX(day), COUNT(*) AS len
  FROM k GROUP BY u, g ORDER BY u, MIN(day)""").fetchall()
print("all streaks (user, start, end, len):", streaks)
print("users with >= 3 days:", sorted({s[0] for s in streaks if s[3] >= 3}))
longest = {}
for u, s, e, n in streaks:
    longest[u] = max(longest.get(u, 0), n)
print("longest streak per user:", longest)

followUps:
Reduce logins to one row per user per day, then check that the latest island ends today (or yesterday if today is still in progress). That island's length is the current streak.

SELECT user_id, COUNT(*) AS len
FROM k GROUP BY user_id, grp
HAVING MAX(day) >= CURRENT_DATE - 1
   AND MAX(day) <= CURRENT_DATE;

Example: days Jan 3, 4, 5 and today Jan 5 give a current streak of 3. If the last login was Jan 3, the current streak is 0 because the island ended before yesterday. State which rule you use (today only, or today or yesterday).

Allowing one missed day means a gap of 2 days still joins runs together. Use technique B: flag a new streak only when the gap to the previous login is more than 2 days, then number streaks with a running sum.

flag = CASE WHEN LAG(day) OVER w IS NULL
            OR day - LAG(day) OVER w > 2
            THEN 1 ELSE 0 END

Example: days 1, 2, 4, 5 have gaps 1, 2, 1, so one streak spanning day 1 to 5 with 4 active days. The value-minus-row-number trick cannot do this, because the difference is no longer constant after a skipped day.

code.title: Sessionize a clickstream with a 30 minute timeout
code.python:
import sqlite3

db = sqlite3.connect(":memory:")
db.execute("CREATE TABLE ev(user_id TEXT, ts INT, id INT)")  # ts in seconds
rows = [("a", 0, 1), ("a", 600, 2), ("a", 1200, 3), ("a", 3100, 4),
        ("a", 3100, 5), ("b", 50, 6)]
db.executemany("INSERT INTO ev VALUES (?,?,?)", rows)
print("events (user, ts, id):", rows)

q = """
WITH f AS (   -- 1 when this event starts a new session
  SELECT user_id, ts, id,
    CASE WHEN LAG(ts) OVER w IS NULL OR ts - LAG(ts) OVER w > 1800 THEN 1 ELSE 0 END AS nw
  FROM ev WINDOW w AS (PARTITION BY user_id ORDER BY ts, id)),
s AS (        -- running sum of the flag numbers the sessions
  SELECT *, SUM(nw) OVER (PARTITION BY user_id ORDER BY ts, id) AS sn FROM f)
SELECT user_id, sn, MIN(ts), MAX(ts), MAX(ts) - MIN(ts) AS dur, COUNT(*) AS events
FROM s GROUP BY user_id, sn ORDER BY user_id, sn"""
print("sessions (user, no, start, end, duration, events):")
for r in db.execute(q):
    print(r)
# Ties on ts are broken by id so the order is deterministic

followUps:
A single-event session has duration 0, which drags a plain average down even though the user did look at a page. So report it in a way that does not hide them.

Options: average only sessions with 2 or more events and report the bounce rate (share of single-event sessions) beside it, use the median, or credit a fixed time (say 30 seconds) to the last event of every session. Example: durations 0, 0, 0, 600 give a mean of 150, a median of 0, and a multi-event average of 600. Say which one the dashboard shows.

Make the output a pure function of the raw events, then replace results instead of appending. Reprocess a whole partition (for example one day plus a look-back of 30 minutes) and overwrite it, using MERGE or delete-then-insert in one transaction.

Give each session a deterministic id, such as a hash of user id and the session's first event id, so a rerun produces the same key and updates rather than duplicates. Example: running the same day twice should leave the row count unchanged. Sort ties by event id so the order never changes between runs.

code.title: Loose funnel versus strict ordered funnel
code.python:
import sqlite3

db = sqlite3.connect(":memory:")
db.execute("CREATE TABLE ev(u TEXT, step TEXT, t INT)")
rows = [("u1", "view", 1), ("u1", "cart", 2), ("u1", "buy", 3),
        ("u2", "cart", 1), ("u2", "view", 2), ("u2", "buy", 3),
        ("u3", "view", 1)]
db.executemany("INSERT INTO ev VALUES (?,?,?)", rows)
print("events:", rows)

# Loose: distinct users per step, order ignored
loose = db.execute("SELECT step, COUNT(DISTINCT u) FROM ev GROUP BY step").fetchall()
print("loose:", sorted(loose))

# Strict: each step must happen after the previous step's time
strict = """
WITH s1 AS (SELECT u, MIN(t) t FROM ev WHERE step='view' GROUP BY u),
s2 AS (SELECT e.u, MIN(e.t) t FROM ev e JOIN s1 ON e.u=s1.u
       WHERE e.step='cart' AND e.t > s1.t GROUP BY e.u),
s3 AS (SELECT e.u, MIN(e.t) t FROM ev e JOIN s2 ON e.u=s2.u
       WHERE e.step='buy' AND e.t > s2.t GROUP BY e.u)
SELECT (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM s1), (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM s2), (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM s3)"""
print("strict view, cart, buy:", db.execute(strict).fetchone())
# u2 bought but carted before viewing, so strict drops u2 at step 2

followUps:
Partition by user and session id, and require every step's time to fall in the same session as step 1. First assign session ids (a gap above 30 minutes starts a new one), then join each step on both user and session id.

JOIN s1 ON e.user_id = s1.user_id
       AND e.session_id = s1.session_id
       AND e.t > s1.t

Example: a view at 10:00 and a purchase the next day count as a funnel completion in a user-level funnel but not in a session-level one. Count the funnel per session if the unit is the session.

For each user who finished the funnel, compute the time from step 1 to the last step, then take the median of those durations. SQL engines without a MEDIAN function need the ROW_NUMBER method or PERCENTILE_CONT(0.5).

SELECT PERCENTILE_CONT(0.5) WITHIN GROUP
  (ORDER BY s3.t - s1.t) FROM s1 JOIN s3 USING (user_id);

Example: durations 2, 3, 100 minutes give a median of 3 where the mean would be about 35, so the median is not distorted by a few slow users. Only converters have a duration, so say so (non-converters are censored).

code.title: Monthly retention cohorts with month index offsets
code.python:
import sqlite3

db = sqlite3.connect(":memory:")
db.executescript("""
CREATE TABLE users(id INT, signup TEXT);
CREATE TABLE act(id INT, m TEXT);
INSERT INTO users VALUES (1,'2023-12'),(2,'2023-12'),(3,'2024-01');
INSERT INTO act VALUES (1,'2023-12'),(1,'2024-01'),(1,'2024-01'),(2,'2023-12'),
                       (3,'2024-01'),(3,'2024-02');
""")

# month index = year*12 + month, so Dec -> Jan is offset 1
idx = lambda c: "(CAST(substr(%s,1,4) AS INT)*12 + CAST(substr(%s,6,2) AS INT))" % (c, c)
q = """
WITH a AS (SELECT DISTINCT id, %s AS mi FROM act),       -- DISTINCT stops double counting
c AS (SELECT id, signup, %s AS ci FROM users),
size AS (SELECT signup, COUNT(*) n FROM c GROUP BY signup)
SELECT c.signup, a.mi - c.ci AS off, COUNT(DISTINCT a.id) AS active, size.n,
       ROUND(100.0 * COUNT(DISTINCT a.id) / size.n) AS pct
FROM c JOIN a ON a.id = c.id JOIN size ON size.signup = c.signup
GROUP BY c.signup, off ORDER BY c.signup, off""" % (idx("m"), idx("signup"))
print("cohort offset active cohort_size pct")
for r in db.execute(q):
    print(*r)
# Denominator is the cohort size from users, not the active count

followUps:
Unbounded retention counts a user as retained in month N if they were active in month N or at any later time, not only in exactly month N. So the curve never goes up as N grows, while "classic" or bracket retention can rise and fall.

Compute it by taking each user's last active offset and counting users whose last offset is at least N: COUNT(CASE WHEN last_off >= N THEN 1 END). Example: a user active in months 0 and 3 counts in unbounded retention at N = 1, 2 and 3, but in classic retention only at N = 0 and 3. It is useful for products with irregular use.

Use percentages, not counts, and show how many users are in each cohort, so a small cohort's swings are visible. Compare the same offset across cohorts, and mark offsets not yet observed as NULL, not 0.

Example: a cohort of 20 users with 10 retained (50%) is far less reliable than 500 of 1,000 (50%), so add a confidence interval or only compare cohorts above a minimum size (say 100). Weighted averages across cohorts use the total retained over the total cohort size, not an average of percentages.

code.title: Median without a MEDIAN function
code.python:
import sqlite3

db = sqlite3.connect(":memory:")
db.execute("CREATE TABLE t(g TEXT, x INT)")
rows = [("a", 5), ("a", 1), ("a", 3), ("b", 8), ("b", 2), ("b", 4), ("b", 6), ("b", None)]
db.executemany("INSERT INTO t VALUES (?,?)", rows)
print("rows:", rows)

# Number rows, count rows, keep the middle one (odd) or two (even), average them
q = """
WITH r AS (
  SELECT g, x,
         ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY g ORDER BY x) AS rn,
         COUNT(*)     OVER (PARTITION BY g) AS c
  FROM t WHERE x IS NOT NULL)          -- drop NULLs before counting
SELECT g, AVG(x) FROM r
WHERE rn IN ((c + 1) / 2, (c + 2) / 2)   -- integer division
GROUP BY g ORDER BY g"""
print("medians:", db.execute(q).fetchall())  # a -> 3.0, b -> (4+6)/2 = 5.0
# Time O(n log n) for the sort, space O(n)

followUps:
P95 is the value below which 95% of rows fall. Use PERCENTILE_CONT(0.95) or PERCENTILE_DISC(0.95) where available; otherwise use the row-number method with a position.

WITH r AS (SELECT x, ROW_NUMBER() OVER (ORDER BY x) rn,
                  COUNT(*) OVER () c FROM t)
SELECT MIN(x) FROM r WHERE rn >= CEIL(0.95 * c);

Example: 100 values give position 95, so the 95th smallest. DISC returns an actual value from the data, CONT interpolates between neighbours, so for 10 values the two can differ slightly.

You cannot merge medians because the median of part medians is not the median of the whole data. SUM and COUNT combine from partial results; the median needs every value's position.

Example: group A has 1, 2, 3 (median 2) and group B has 10, 11 (median 10.5). Averaging the medians gives 6.25, but the true median of 1, 2, 3, 10, 11 is 3. So a distributed engine must shuffle all values to one place, or use mergeable sketches instead.

A t-digest is most accurate at the tails and less accurate near the median, because it keeps small clusters at the extremes. That is why it suits P99 and P99.9.

The error is relative to rank, not value: for P99 the rank error is typically a small fraction of a percent, but with very few values (say fewer than 100) it can be off by a whole data point. The extreme values (min and max) are stored exactly. Compression is a setting; a typical value like 100 uses a few kilobytes and bounds the centroid count, trading memory for accuracy.

Alert on a sketch-based P99 by merging the per-minute sketches over a window (say 5 minutes), reading P99 from the merged sketch, and firing when it stays above the limit for several windows in a row. Never average per-minute P99 values, because percentiles do not average.

Example: limit 500 ms, window 5 minutes, fire after 3 breaches in a row. Allow for the sketch's error by adding a margin or checking the sample count, and also alert on a count of requests above 500 ms, which can be computed exactly.

code.title: Pivot rows to columns with conditional aggregation
code.python:
import sqlite3

db = sqlite3.connect(":memory:")
db.execute("CREATE TABLE sales(region TEXT, quarter TEXT, revenue INT)")
rows = [("east", "Q1", 10), ("east", "Q2", 20), ("east", "Q2", 5),
        ("west", "Q1", 7), ("west", "Q3", 9)]
db.executemany("INSERT INTO sales VALUES (?,?,?)", rows)
print("long format:", rows)

# One CASE per output column; GROUP BY makes one row per region
q = """
SELECT region,
       SUM(CASE WHEN quarter='Q1' THEN revenue END) AS q1,
       SUM(CASE WHEN quarter='Q2' THEN revenue END) AS q2,
       COALESCE(SUM(CASE WHEN quarter='Q3' THEN revenue END), 0) AS q3
FROM sales GROUP BY region ORDER BY region"""
print("wide format (region, q1, q2, q3):")
for r in db.execute(q):
    print(r)    # missing cells are NULL (None) unless wrapped in COALESCE

# Unpivot: one SELECT per column glued with UNION ALL
u = """SELECT region, 'Q1' q, q1 FROM w UNION ALL SELECT region, 'Q2', q2 FROM w"""
db.execute("CREATE TABLE w AS " + q)
print("unpivot:", db.execute(u + " ORDER BY 1, 2").fetchall())

followUps:
SQL Server's PIVOT groups by every column of the source that you did not name in the PIVOT, so any extra column silently becomes part of the group key and splits your rows. You get several rows per region instead of one.

Example: if the source also has an id column, each id is its own group and nothing collapses. Fix by selecting only the needed columns in a derived table first: FROM (SELECT region, quarter, revenue FROM sales) s PIVOT (SUM(revenue) FOR quarter IN ([Q1],[Q2])) p. The column list in IN must also be written out in advance.

A wide table is a good storage design when the set of columns is small and fixed, and queries read the whole row: reporting tables, feature tables for machine learning, and a pre-pivoted summary that feeds a dashboard.

It is a bad design when columns are open-ended (new product every week means a schema change) or when most cells are NULL. Example: 12 monthly columns is fine, 5,000 sparse attribute columns is not. Narrow (long) tables keep the schema stable and are easy to filter and aggregate; pivot at query or report time.

code.title: Recursive CTE walking an org chart
code.python:
import sqlite3

db = sqlite3.connect(":memory:")
db.execute("CREATE TABLE emp(id INT, name TEXT, manager_id INT)")
rows = [(1, "CEO", None), (2, "VP", 1), (3, "Dev", 2), (4, "Ops", 2), (5, "Intern", 3)]
db.executemany("INSERT INTO emp VALUES (?,?,?)", rows)
print("employees:", rows)

q = """
WITH RECURSIVE org(id, name, depth, path) AS (
  SELECT id, name, 0, name FROM emp WHERE manager_id IS NULL      -- anchor, runs once
  UNION ALL
  SELECT e.id, e.name, o.depth + 1, o.path || ' > ' || e.name     -- recursive member
  FROM emp e JOIN org o ON e.manager_id = o.id                    -- joins previous level only
  WHERE o.depth < 10)                                             -- guard against cycles
SELECT depth, path FROM org ORDER BY path"""
for d, p in db.execute(q):
    print("  " * d + p)
# Each round is one set of probes on manager_id; stops when a round returns no rows

followUps:
Compute it with a recursive CTE that carries each employee's salary down to the root, or better, make every employee carry its own root path. The simplest way is to generate all (manager, descendant) pairs, then sum.

WITH RECURSIVE t(boss, id) AS (
  SELECT id, id FROM emp
  UNION ALL
  SELECT t.boss, e.id FROM emp e JOIN t ON e.manager_id = t.id)
SELECT t.boss, SUM(e.salary) FROM t JOIN emp e ON e.id = t.id GROUP BY t.boss;

Each person is their own descendant, so a manager's total includes their own pay. Example: CEO 100, VP 50, Dev 30 gives totals CEO 180, VP 80, Dev 30.

Adjacency list stores only a manager_id per row: simple to write and update, but subtree queries need a recursive CTE. Nested sets store left and right numbers, so a subtree is one range query, but inserts renumber many rows. A closure table stores every (ancestor, descendant, depth) pair, so subtree and path queries are plain joins, at the cost of O(n x depth) extra rows.

Example: a 3-level chain of 3 nodes has 2 adjacency edges and 6 closure rows (3 self pairs plus 3 ancestor pairs). Choose adjacency for changing trees, closure for heavy reads.

code.title: Delete duplicates but keep one copy, previewed first
code.python:
import sqlite3

db = sqlite3.connect(":memory:")
db.execute("CREATE TABLE users(id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, email TEXT)")
emails = ["a@x.com", "A@x.com ", "b@x.com", "a@x.com", "b@x.com"]
db.executemany("INSERT INTO users(email) VALUES (?)", [(e,) for e in emails])
print("before:", db.execute("SELECT * FROM users").fetchall())

# Rank rows inside each normalised key; the lowest id survives
victims = """
SELECT id FROM (
  SELECT id, ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY LOWER(TRIM(email)) ORDER BY id) AS rn
  FROM users) WHERE rn > 1"""
print("preview of ids to delete:", [r[0] for r in db.execute(victims)])

with db:   # one transaction: commits only if the DELETE succeeds
    db.execute("DELETE FROM users WHERE id IN (" + victims + ")")
print("after: ", db.execute("SELECT * FROM users").fetchall())
db.execute("CREATE UNIQUE INDEX ux ON users(email)")  # stops new exact duplicates

followUps:
With NOT IN, a single NULL in the subquery makes every comparison unknown, so the whole filter returns no rows. x NOT IN (1, 2, NULL) is never true: it means x <> 1 AND x <> 2 AND x <> NULL, and the last part is unknown.

Example: DELETE FROM users WHERE id NOT IN (SELECT MIN(id) FROM users GROUP BY email) is safe only if the subquery never returns NULL. If ids can be NULL, nothing is deleted, with no error. Use NOT EXISTS instead, which handles NULL as expected, or filter with WHERE id IS NOT NULL.

Fuzzy duplicates need a similarity measure and a human or a threshold, not a simple key. Normalise first (lower case, trim, strip punctuation), then compare candidates only within a cheap block such as the same postcode or first letter, so you do not compare all pairs.

Score pairs with edit distance, trigram similarity (PostgreSQL pg_trgm) or SOUNDEX. Example: "Jon" and "John" are 1 edit apart, a close match; flag pairs above 0.8 similarity for review, merge the sure ones and re-point foreign keys to the survivor. Never auto-delete on a fuzzy match.

code.title: Triple self-join versus window approach for 3 consecutive days
code.python:
import sqlite3

db = sqlite3.connect(":memory:")
db.execute("CREATE TABLE l(u INT, day INT)")   # day numbers
rows = [(1, 1), (1, 2), (1, 3), (1, 4), (1, 5), (2, 1), (2, 3), (2, 4)]
db.executemany("INSERT INTO l VALUES (?,?)", rows)
print("logins:", rows)

# Self-join: fixed K=3, long streaks match many times, needs DISTINCT
sj = db.execute("""
  SELECT a.u, COUNT(*) AS matches FROM l a
  JOIN l b ON b.u = a.u AND b.day = a.day + 1
  JOIN l c ON c.u = a.u AND c.day = a.day + 2
  GROUP BY a.u""").fetchall()
print("self-join matches per user (user 1 has 3 matches for one streak):", sj)

# Window: one pass gives every streak, any K, and the length
win = db.execute("""
  WITH k AS (SELECT u, day, day - ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY u ORDER BY day) g FROM l)
  SELECT u, MIN(day), MAX(day), COUNT(*) FROM k GROUP BY u, g ORDER BY u""").fetchall()
print("streaks (user, start, end, len):", win)

followUps:
A self-join is reasonable for a fixed, small check on small data, or when each link needs a different condition that a window function cannot express, such as joining two different tables or matching on more than day order.

Example: "find users who logged in on day D and D+1" is one join and easy to read. It also helps when an index makes the join cheap and the table is small. It stops being reasonable as K grows, as streak length matters, or as rows multiply: with K = 7 you need 6 joins and long streaks produce many repeated matches.

In a columnar warehouse the self-join becomes several large distributed hash joins, each shuffling the whole table by user id, so it moves much more data. The window version needs one shuffle by user, one sort inside each partition, and one pass.

Columnar storage reads only the user and day columns, which helps both, but the window plan scans once while a K-way self-join scans K times. Example: 1 billion rows, K = 7 means 7 scans and 6 shuffles against 1 scan and 1 shuffle. Check with EXPLAIN and the bytes shuffled.

Keep a small per-user state table (current streak length and last login day) and update it from only the new day's logins, instead of recomputing from history.

new_len = CASE WHEN last_day = today - 1 THEN len + 1
               WHEN last_day = today     THEN len
               ELSE 1 END

Example: yesterday a user had a streak of 4 ending yesterday; they log in today, so the streak is 5. If they did not log in, the stored streak is cleared by a job that compares last_day to today. Run as a MERGE into the state table, so it is O(new rows) per day, not O(all history).

Data skew means a few keys hold most of the rows, so one worker gets far more data than the rest. PARTITION BY sends all rows with the same key to the same worker, so one huge user (a bot with 500 million events) makes a single task run for hours while others finish quickly, and it can run out of memory when sorting.

Fixes: filter or cap bots, split by a secondary key such as day when the logic allows, salt the key for aggregations (not for ordered windows), or handle the heavy keys in a separate query. Check the stage timings for one slow task.

Give the model the table schema, the exact definition of correct output, and ask for rows that break the common mistakes. Example prompt:

Given events(user_id, event_time, event_id), generate INSERT statements for 12 rows that include: two events at the same timestamp, a gap of exactly 30 minutes, a gap of 30 minutes 1 second, an event just after midnight, a user with one event, and a user with events out of order in the file. For each user write the expected number of sessions.

The expected answers let you check the query without trusting it.

Validate on a small, safe slice first, never by running unreviewed code on production. Use a read-only role, limit to one day or a sample of users, and run EXPLAIN before the query to check cost.

Then run your own version and the AI version on the same slice and compare row counts and a checksum, for example SELECT COUNT(*), SUM(session_no), and inspect every differing row. Example: if one query returns 1,204 sessions and the other 1,198, the 6 rows that differ usually reveal a tie or a timezone definition. Only then widen the date range.
